metadata.file_name: 64. Constante-Amores et al. (2024). Contribution of machine learning to the analysis of grade repetition in Spain: A study based on PISA data.pdf
metadata.title: Contribution of machine learning to the analysis of grade repetition in Spain: A study based on PISA data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Spain microdata with a two-stage sampling design and reports both unweighted and weighted grade-repetition rates in Table 1, indicating that the authors were aware of the complex survey structure. However, in the machine-learning workflow (training/validation split, AUC-based model selection, and stochastic gradient boosting), the manuscript does not explicitly state which PISA student weight variable was applied in the ML fitting or whether weights were used at all. For the subsequent multilevel binary logistic regression, the paper reports multilevel structure (students within schools) and model fit statistics, but it does not specify the exact PISA weight variable or replicate-weight method. Therefore, weighting is not clearly documented for the predictive ML stage; analysts should consult the linked annexes and OECD PISA technical documentation to confirm whether weights were applied consistently across ML and multilevel models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variables are dichotomous self-reports of grade repetition (primary and secondary), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The paper does, however, explicitly address missingness in predictors using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), so missing-data handling is documented for the modeling inputs.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of PISA 2018 Spain. The initial Spanish PISA 2018 student sample is 35,943 (two-stage sampling; 92% coverage of 15-year-olds). For the multilevel logistic regression objective, the authors removed schools with fewer than 20 subjects, excluding 1,532 students from 133 centres, yielding a final multilevel analytic sample of 34,411 students. For the ML stage, the paper reports preprocessing (multiple imputation, centring/scaling) and a random 70%/30% train/validation split, but it does not specify additional grade- or item-level exclusions beyond the multilevel school-size restriction.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Spain (compulsory education) — primary grade repetition (self-report)
main_findings.target_variable: Grade repetition in primary education (ever repeated)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stochastic Gradient Boosting selected as most accurate (AUC on validation set; exact AUC values not reported). Multilevel logistic regression: Model 1 PEV=62.380%, Model 4 PEV=61% with best fit (lowest AIC/BIC; variance reduction vs null model reported as R2≈9% compared to model 1).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), expected occupational status, and learning time for mathematics (plus school-change and teacher-instruction variables) to predict whether students had repeated a grade in primary education, finding that social status and learning-time indicators were among the strongest correlates and that the full multilevel model explained about 61% of the variance (PEV). This indicates that equity-oriented supports in early primary schooling should prioritize compensatory resources and learning-time management, while also addressing classroom instructional practices and student expectations, though the results are correlational and do not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Spain (compulsory education) — secondary grade repetition (self-report)
main_findings.target_variable: Grade repetition in secondary education (ever repeated)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stochastic Gradient Boosting selected as most accurate (AUC on validation set; exact AUC values not reported). Multilevel logistic regression: Model 4 PEV=55.69% with best fit (lowest AIC/BIC); variance reduction vs model 1 reported as R2≈10.298% and vs null model as 5% (models 2 and 3: 10% and 5% respectively).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged expected occupational status, learning time for sciences, and socioeconomic status (along with student behaviour hindering learning and perceived test difficulty) to predict whether students had repeated a grade in secondary education, finding that the strongest effects combined student background with school-related learning-time and classroom/behaviour factors and that the global multilevel model explained about 55.69% of the variance (PEV). This indicates that secondary-grade repetition prevention should combine learning-time and instructional/behaviour supports with interventions targeting students’ expectations and perceived academic difficulty, while recognizing that the study’s design is exploratory and does not imply causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 Spain (n=35,943; two-stage sampling) to model grade repetition in primary and secondary education as dichotomous self-reports. For variable selection, it compares four supervised ML algorithms (CART/C5.0, random forest, and stochastic gradient boosting) using AUC with 10-fold cross-validation on a 70% training / 30% validation split; stochastic gradient boosting is selected as the most accurate and used to rank the most informative predictors. The authors then estimate multilevel binary logistic regression models (students nested in schools) after multiple imputation by chained equations and after excluding schools with fewer than 20 subjects (final multilevel sample: 34,411). In primary education, the best global model (M4) reaches PEV≈61% with the lowest AIC/BIC and an R2≈9% variance reduction relative to model 1; in secondary education, M4 reaches PEV≈55.69% with R2≈10.298% relative to model 1. Limitations include the absence of explicit causal identification and incomplete reporting of ML weighting/complex-survey handling details; relationships are therefore correlational.
